claim: Using local materials instead of bringing everything from Earth is what NASA calls In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU): collecting, processing, storing and using materials found on the Moon, for example turning water ice into breathable oxygen or getting metal for building. A NASA-hosted paper says lunar regolith contains approximately 45% oxygen by mass; the oxygen is not a gas but is bound in the minerals (NASA, 2026: oxygen 'molecularly bonded to rock and dust'). NASA's Carbothermal Reduction Demonstration (CaRD) heats regolith with carbon so the oxygen leaves the rock as carbon monoxide (and carbon dioxide); other, already proven steps then turn that into oxygen. Tests: (1) on 25 April 2023 NASA reported that a team at Johnson Space Center in Houston had melted lunar soil simulant with a high-powered laser (standing in for concentrated sunlight) inside a carbothermal reactor built by Sierra Space, in JSC's 15-foot (about 4.6 m) Dirty Thermal Vacuum Chamber; the MSolo mass spectrometer detected carbon monoxide, and NASA said the reactor reached technology readiness level 6. (2) In summer 2024 Sierra Space ran its automated reactor again and again in the same chamber at lunar-like vacuum and temperature. (3) A later integrated test used real concentrated sunlight with a NASA Glenn solar concentrator and confirmed carbon monoxide production (NASA article of 13 Feb 2026; test photo dated 7 Aug 2025).
card_en: Astronauts can't carry everything from Earth, so NASA wants to use what is already on the Moon. Moon rock and dust are almost half oxygen (about 45% of their mass), but the oxygen is locked inside the minerals. In 2023 a NASA team melted look-alike Moon soil with a laser inside a vacuum chamber, and the oxygen came out joined to carbon, as a gas called carbon monoxide, which other machines can turn into oxygen to breathe.
card_ru: Астронавты не могут привезти с Земли всё, что нужно, поэтому NASA хочет использовать то, что уже есть на Луне. Лунные камни и пыль почти наполовину состоят из кислорода (около 45% их массы), но он крепко заперт внутри минералов. В 2023 году команда NASA расплавила лазером искусственный лунный грунт в вакуумной камере, и кислород вышел из него вместе с углеродом — в виде угарного газа, из которого другие машины умеют получать кислород для дыхания.

claim: NASA's 3D-Printed Habitat Challenge, a Centennial Challenges competition run with Bradley University, began in 2015 and was completed in May 2019; 60 teams took part and NASA awarded more than $2 million in prize money. In the final head-to-head round (1-4 May 2019, at Caterpillar's Edwards Demonstration & Learning Center in Edwards, Illinois) the teams printed one-third-scale habitats; AI SpaceFactory won the top prize of $500,000 and Pennsylvania State University won $200,000. The company ICON 3D printed Mars Dune Alpha, a 1,700-square-foot (about 158 m2) simulated Martian habitat at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston (ICON won the subcontract in 2021 from Jacobs). NASA's first CHAPEA crew of four volunteers lived in it from 25 June 2023 to 6 July 2024, a mission NASA calls 378 days; a second CHAPEA crew of four lived there from 19 October 2025 to 31 October 2026, also a 378-day mission. In November 2022 NASA gave ICON a $57.2 million SBIR Phase III contract, running through 2028, for its Olympus construction system, which NASA says is 'designed to use local resources on the Moon and Mars as building materials'; in 2020 NASA said ICON would work with NASA Marshall under the MMPACT project 'to test lunar soil simulant with various processing and printing technologies'.
card_en: Big 3D printers can build a house by laying down building material layer after layer. NASA ran a contest for 3D-printed space homes from 2015 to 2019, and later the company ICON printed Mars Dune Alpha, a pretend Mars home of 1,700 square feet (about 158 square metres), in Houston. Two crews of four volunteers have each lived inside it for 378 days, as if they were on Mars.

В нём уже пожили два экипажа по четыре добровольца, каждый по 378 дней, будто на Марсе.

claim: The first 3D printer in space (the 3D Printing in Zero-G technology demonstration, built by Made In Space with NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center) was installed on the International Space Station by Expedition 42 commander Barry 'Butch' Wilmore on 17 November 2014. On 24 November 2014 ground controllers commanded the first printed part: a faceplate of the extruder's casing (NASA: 'the printhead faceplate'), engraved with the names NASA and Made In Space, which showed that the printer can make replacement parts for itself. In December 2014 (NASA photo dated 16 Dec 2014) the printer made a ratchet wrench from a design file sent from the ground; a NASA in-space manufacturing presentation says the file was 'e-mailed', i.e. uplinked. The Refabricator, built by Tethers Unlimited, recycled waste plastic (including earlier printed items) into new printer filament; Anne McClain installed it in February 2019, when it began operations, and NASA says it 'successfully manufactured its first object', with some bonding problems likely caused by microgravity.
card_en: In November 2014 astronaut Butch Wilmore set up the first 3D printer in space, on the International Space Station. Its very first print was a small cover plate for the printer itself, which showed that a printer can make its own spare parts. In December 2014 engineers on Earth sent up the design of a ratchet wrench, and the station printed the tool.

claim: Artemis I (16 November to 11 December 2022, no crew) carried MARE, the Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment: two identical female torso phantoms ('mannequins'), Helga (provided by DLR, no vest, seat 4, the baseline) and Zohar (provided by the Israel Space Agency, wearing the AstroRad vest, seat 3), fitted with passive and active radiation detectors. Results were published in Science Advances on 12 August 2026 (Houri et al.). There was no solar particle event (solar storm) during Artemis I, so the team used measurements from Orion's pass through the inner Van Allen belt and computer models to predict the vest's effect in two big historical storms: effective dose reductions of 60% for an August 1972-like event and nearly 40% for an October 1989-like event (DLR's release also gives 58.2% and 36.9% for virtual full-body phantoms). That could spare astronauts the equivalent of up to 193 and 131 days of deep-space radiation exposure. The flight vest had a high-density polyethylene core made of thousands of hexagonal rods and a mass of 26 kg; it protects red bone marrow, colon, lungs, stomach, breasts and ovaries.
card_en: On the Artemis I flight around the Moon in 2022, two model human bodies named Helga and Zohar rode in the Orion spacecraft, packed with radiation sensors. Only Zohar wore AstroRad, a 26 kg vest made of thousands of small plastic rods. There was no solar storm on the trip, so scientists used the measurements and computer models: in a very strong solar storm the vest would cut the dose by about 40 to 60 percent, depending on the storm.

Только на Зохар надели AstroRad — жилет массой 26 кг из тысяч маленьких пластиковых стерженьков. Солнечной бури в полёте не случилось, поэтому учёные взяли измерения и компьютерные модели: в очень сильную солнечную бурю жилет уменьшил бы дозу радиации примерно на 40–60%, в зависимости от бури.

notes: Status 'verified': the draft is right, and the results it asked about are now published. (1) The numbers are PREDICTIONS, not a measurement during a storm: no solar particle event happened on Artemis I, so the team extrapolated data from Orion's pass through the inner Van Allen belt to two historical storms using computer models. The 60% and 'nearly 40%' are reductions of EFFECTIVE DOSE for August 1972-like and October 1989-like storms, compared with sitting unshielded in Orion's normal cabin (not in the storm shelter). Do NOT write 'the vest blocked 60% of the radiation on Artemis I', and do not apply the numbers to cosmic rays: the paper says solar-storm protons can be weakened by realistic shielding 'unlike' galactic cosmic radiation. (2) The paper's first and last authors work for StemRad, the company that makes the vest (co-authors from DLR, NASA JSC, the Israel Space Agency and Lockheed Martin). (3) Mass: 26 kg. claim: In NASA's Plant Habitat-04 (PH-04) experiment, astronaut Shane Kimbrough put 48 seeds of NuMex 'Española Improved', which NASA calls a hybrid Hatch chile pepper, into the Advanced Plant Habitat (APH) on 12 July 2021. claim: Apollo 16 astronauts John Young (commander) and Charles Duke spent a little under three days on the Moon in April 1972. Young set up the gold-plated Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, designed and built by George R. Carruthers, on a tripod in the shadow of the lunar module in the Descartes highlands. NASA calls it the first Moon-based telescope and 'the first telescope used to make astronomical observations from the surface of another planetary body'. It looked back at Earth and took the very first images of Earth's geocorona from space (the ultraviolet glow of hydrogen in the outermost atmosphere) and of aurorae; it also studied star clusters, nebulae and the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. The astronauts brought back 178 frames of film, and the instrument is still on the Moon. NASA's Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, named after him, launched on 24 September 2025 and reached its orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point in January 2026.
card_en: In April 1972 the Apollo 16 astronauts set up the first telescope on the Moon, a gold-coated camera built by the scientist George Carruthers. It saw ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see, and photographed the glow of Earth's outermost air, called the geocorona, as well as star clusters and a nearby galaxy. The telescope is still standing on the Moon today.

claim: NASA's Vertical Solar Array Technology (VSAT) project, led by NASA Langley with NASA Glenn, develops solar arrays on tall masts for the lunar South Pole, where the Sun does not rise very far above the horizon and long shadows can block flat (horizontal) arrays. In March 2021 NASA picked five companies (Astrobotic, ATK Space Systems/Northrop Grumman, Honeybee Robotics, Lockheed Martin, Space Systems Loral/Maxar) for 12-month design contracts worth up to $700,000 each. In August 2022 NASA chose three to build prototypes and test them, $19.4 million in total: Astrobotic $6.2 million, Honeybee Robotics $7 million, Lockheed Martin $6.2 million. The arrays must deploy by themselves up to 32 feet (about 10 m) high, on uneven ground, and retract so they can be moved; NASA's project documents and its Lunar Surface Technology page say VSAT explores masts of up to 20 m. Power: a 2023 NASA review lists Honeybee's design (LAMPS) at 10 kW, and NASA says regenerative fuel cells plus VSAT can supply and recharge 10 kW. In summer 2024 Honeybee Robotics (a Blue Origin company) and Astrobotic tested their prototypes in Chamber A at NASA Johnson in Houston. Status (November 2026): none has flown; NASA's goal is to deploy at least one near the Moon's South Pole near the end of this decade, and a September 2026 NASA call for proposals lists vertical solar arrays among the technologies to mature and demonstrate.
card_en: At the Moon's south pole the Sun stays low near the horizon, so long shadows can hide flat solar panels. NASA is developing solar panels that rise on a tall mast, about 10 metres high (masts up to 20 metres are being studied), and fold back down so they can be moved. In summer 2024 two companies tested their prototypes in a giant vacuum chamber in Houston, and NASA hopes to set one up near the south pole by the end of this decade.

NASA разрабатывает панели, которые поднимаются на высокой мачте — примерно на 10 метров (изучают и мачты до 20 метров) — и складываются обратно, чтобы их можно было перевезти. claim: Curiosity's ChemCam (Chemistry and Camera), built by a U.S.-French team led by Los Alamos National Laboratory with France's space agency CNES, uses laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy. Each infrared laser pulse delivers more than a million watts for about five billionths of a second and turns a pinhead-size spot on a rock into glowing, ionized gas (plasma); ChemCam's telescope collects the light of that spark and spectrometers (three of them, recording 6,144 wavelengths of ultraviolet, visible and infrared light) analyse its spectrum to identify the elements, because different elements glow in different wavelengths, or colours. It zaps rock and soil targets up to about 23 feet (7 m) away, usually 30 pulses at each of several points. Its first shot on Mars hit the rock 'Coronation' (reported 19 Aug 2012); it passed 100,000 shots by December 2013 and fired its 1 millionth shot on sol 4281 (August 2024) at the target Royce Lake. Perseverance's SuperCam does a similar job; NASA says it can identify the chemical and mineral makeup of spots as small as a pencil point from more than 20 feet (7 m) away.
card_en: The Curiosity rover carries a laser called ChemCam that zaps rocks up to 7 metres away and turns a pinhead-sized spot into a tiny glowing spark. Each chemical element glows in its own colours, so the light from the spark tells scientists what the rock is made of. By August 2024 ChemCam had fired its laser one million times, and the Perseverance rover carries a similar tool called SuperCam.

Каждый химический элемент светится своими цветами, поэтому по свету искры учёные узнают, из чего состоит камень. К августу 2024 года ChemCam выстрелил лазером миллион раз, а у марсохода Perseverance есть похожий прибор — SuperCam.

claim: NASA's Perseverance rover filmed Phobos, Mars' potato-shaped moon, crossing the face of the Sun with its Mastcam-Z camera on 2 April 2022, the mission's 397th Martian day (sol). The eclipse lasted a little over 40 seconds, much shorter than a typical solar eclipse by Earth's Moon; NASA calls it the most zoomed-in, highest-frame-rate observation of a Phobos solar eclipse ever taken from the Martian surface. Phobos is getting closer to Mars and is destined to crash into the planet in tens of millions of years. claim: The space station spacesuit (EMU) has a backpack (Primary Life Support System, PLSS) that keeps the astronaut at a safe temperature, provides oxygen and removes carbon dioxide and humidity. NASA's Inspector General (2017) says it provides oxygen 'for up to 7 hours' and calls 7 hours the EMU's maximum per spacewalk; a NASA-hosted operations briefing (2014) says the suit carries consumables for a spacewalk of 7 hours at most (15 minutes out, 6 hours of work, 15 minutes back in, 30 minutes of reserve). If the backpack fails, a separate secondary oxygen pack gives at least 30 minutes of emergency oxygen. NASA's spacesuit page says spacewalks typically last six to eight hours. A 2023 conference paper on NASA's server gives the ISS suit's capacity as 8 hours nominally (longest use 8.93 hours, about 8 h 56 min). Apollo 15-17 suits: primary life support 'certified' for 7 hours (longest use 7.62 hours) with a 30-minute backup (the Oxygen Purge System); the longest Apollo moonwalk, Apollo 17's second, lasted 7 hours 37 minutes (NASA).
card_en: A spacesuit backpack works like a tiny spaceship: it gives the astronaut oxygen, keeps them cool and cleans the air they breathe out. The space station suit carries oxygen for about 7 hours, plus an emergency pack with 30 more minutes, and spacewalks usually last 6 to 8 hours. On Apollo 17 in 1972, one moonwalk lasted 7 hours and 37 minutes.

claim: The Apollo Lunar Surface Drill was a battery-powered rotary-percussion drill (280 rotations and 2,270 blows per minute). It was flown on Apollo 13, 15, 16 and 17 (Apollo 13 did not land, so it was used on Apollo 15, 16 and 17) so that one astronaut could drill two holes for heat-flow probes (planned 3 m deep) and collect a 2-3 m deep core of lunar soil in hollow drill stems about 40 cm long. NASA's lunar sample curator lists the deep drill cores as 236 cm (Apollo 15), 224 cm (Apollo 16) and 305 cm (Apollo 17), and says drilling was shown to be possible down to 3 m. Curiosity's drill makes holes 0.63 inch (1.6 cm) wide: its first sample hole, in the rock 'John Klein' on 8 Feb 2013 (sol 182), was 2.5 inches (6.4 cm) deep - the first time any robot drilled into a rock to collect a sample on Mars - and the 'Windjana' hole (5 May 2014) was about 2.6 inches (6.5 cm) deep.
card_en: On the last three Apollo missions, astronauts dug into the Moon with a battery-powered drill that spun and hammered at the same time. Its hollow tubes brought back columns of Moon soil 2 to 3 metres long. The Curiosity rover's drill on Mars makes much smaller holes: 1.6 cm wide and about 6.5 cm deep.

Её полые трубки достали столбики лунного грунта длиной 2–3 метра. Бур марсохода Curiosity делает на Марсе отверстия гораздо меньше: шириной 1,6 см и глубиной около 6,5 см.

claim: Best-sourced example: on 3 May 2017 ESA reported that bricks had been 3D printed out of simulated moondust using concentrated sunlight, at the solar furnace of the DLR German Aerospace Center in Cologne. As a baseline, 147 curved mirrors focus sunlight into a high-temperature beam that melts the soil grains together; the 3D printer baked successive 0.1 mm layers of moondust at 1000°C, and a 20 x 10 x 3 cm brick took around five hours. The bricks have the equivalent strength of gypsum. The simulant was a commercially available simulated lunar soil based on volcanic material from Earth, and the test ran in normal air (standard atmospheric conditions), not in lunar vacuum. ESA notes that only the 3D printer and a solar concentrator would need to go to the Moon (an earlier method needed a binding salt). NASA is also funding this kind of work: Mason, a NASA Tipping Point investment with Redwire Space, combines a grader, compactor and microwave emitter that removes rocks, compacts loose regolith and melts or sinters it into a solid surface for landing pads, roads and habitat foundations.
card_en: Bricks for a Moon base could be made from Moon dust and sunshine. In 2017 a team in Europe used 147 curved mirrors to focus sunlight and bake look-alike Moon dust at 1000 °C, one layer of 0.1 mm at a time. A brick 20 × 10 × 3 cm took about five hours and came out as strong as gypsum (plaster).

Кирпич размером 20 × 10 × 3 см печатался около пяти часов и получился прочным, как гипс.

claim: Lunar regolith is made of the same major rock-forming elements as Earth's rocks: oxygen, silicon, aluminum, calcium, magnesium and iron. In the highlands, plagioclase feldspar accumulated in a rock called anorthosite; a 1979 NASA JSC assessment says the plagioclase mineral anorthite, containing 19% aluminum and 20% silicon, can be concentrated from some highland soils where it makes up to 60%. The mare basalts contain ilmenite, an iron-titanium oxide; ilmenite containing 32% titanium and 37% iron can be concentrated from some mare soils, where it makes up to 10%. Impacts left very-fine-grained droplets or spheres of iron metal (Fe0) in the glass of lunar soil, typically 4-33 nanometres in size ('nanophase iron'); micrometeorite impacts also make thin glassy rims on grains that contain nanophase iron. NASA projects aim to get metals and oxygen from regolith (Molten Regolith Electrolysis; Blue Alchemist, which aims to produce silicon solar cells, aluminum wires, oxygen, iron and slag), and carbothermal oxygen production leaves a slag that contains the reduced metals. On Mars, NASA says iron minerals in the dirt oxidize, or rust, which makes the surface look red.
card_en: Moon soil is made of the same main elements as rocks on Earth, including the metals aluminium and iron. The highlands are rich in a mineral full of aluminium, the dark lava plains contain ilmenite, made of iron, titanium and oxygen, and tiny meteorite hits have even left specks of iron metal, far too small to see. Mars looks red because iron in its dust has rusted.

На лунных возвышенностях много минерала, богатого алюминием, в тёмных лавовых равнинах есть ильменит — минерал из железа, титана и кислорода, а крошечные метеориты при ударах даже оставили в пыли частички металлического железа, слишком маленькие, чтобы их разглядеть. Марс выглядит красным, потому что железо в его пыли заржавело.

(1) The draft's 'tiny native iron beads from meteorite impacts' is right in kind, but NASA's guide says these droplets are 'typically 4-33 nm in size', i.e. billionths of a metre: far too small to see or pick up. (3) The same 1979 abstract warns that 'bulk lunar soil is not a suitable feedstock for extracting metals' unless minerals such as anorthite and ilmenite are separated first; NASA's MRE and Blue Alchemist pages describe plans, not working factories.
